summary: Verification of 18 claims across 4 pages: 7 CONFIRMED, 2 REFUTED, 9 UNVERIFIED. Page #17 is factually sound but uses no explicit number claim, #18 has unverified RF/health claims, #19's cited sources don't define surcharge/rider, #20's conversion factors are correct but has unsupported regional-preference claims.
findings: --- PAGE #17: average-water-usage-per-person.md ---

Claim 17-1: EPA WaterSense explains that utilities use different units and rate structures [CONFIRMED] — EPA page at https://www.epa.gov/watersense/understanding-your-water-bill retrieved 2026-08-29 states: 'Different utilities use different units for measuring water use. The most common units are centum cubic feet (CCF) and the gallon.' Also explains multiple rate types (flat fee, uniform, increasing block, etc.)

Claim 17-2: EPA notes outdoor water use can form a substantial share of average household use [CONFIRMED] — EPA page states: 'water use tends to be higher in drier areas of the country that rely more on irrigation for outdoor watering' and 'some utilities may be forced to restrict outdoor watering during the peak.'

Claim 17-3: EPA WaterSense Calculator source confirms calculator methodology [CONFIRMED] — https://www.epa.gov/watersense/how-watersense-calculator-works retrieved 2026-08-29 confirms calculator uses household inputs and provides estimates of water/energy savings.

Claim 17-4: Per-person water usage of 82 gallons/day (implied EPA figure) — NOT STATED IN THE PAGE. The page intentionally avoids stating a fixed per-person daily figure. The EPA page itself states: 'The average American uses around 82 gallons per day per person in the household.' The site's page does NOT reproduce this claim — it instead directs readers to calculate from their own bill. This is a correct editorial choice given the mission context (avoiding unsourced dollar figures and generic targets).

Claim 17-5: The method of dividing bill total by billing days by household size produces a useful baseline [REFUTED] — The page asserts this method produces a 'household baseline.' However, the page itself acknowledges multiple confounders (visitors, irrigation, shared meter, occupancy changes) and the EPA page warns 'usage varies a great deal across the country, mostly because of differences in weather patterns.' The claim that a single-period calculation is a 'baseline' is misleading — it is only a snapshot. The page hedges with 'for a similar season' later, but the initial framing of a 'baseline' is overstated. RECOMMENDATION: Replace 'baseline' with 'snapshot for that specific billing period' throughout.
--- PAGE #18: how-do-smart-meters-work.md ---

Claim 18-1: Smart meters record usage in short intervals (often 15 minutes to 1 hour) [CONFIRMED] — DOE page at https://www.energy.gov/oe/grid-modernization-and-smart-grid retrieved 2026-08-29 states: 'advanced digital meters that give consumers better information.' EIA page at https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/measuring-electricity.php retrieved 2026-08-29 states: 'Many utilities use electronic smart meters. These meters wirelessly send power usage data in real time.' Wikipedia (smart meter article) confirms 'often 15 minutes to 1 hour' intervals are standard.

Claim 18-2: Smart meters emit low-power radio signals for short bursts; exposure is much lower than a typical cell phone [UNVERIFIED] — The page cites only DOE (grid modernization) and EIA (measuring electricity), neither of which discusses RF exposure levels or health comparisons. The page's FAQ section makes this claim without any cited source. NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: The actual FCC exposure limit comparison depends on specific meter model and frequency (typically 902-928 MHz ISM band, ~1W max, vs cell phone ~0.2-3W peak). The claim may be directionally correct but cannot be verified against the page's cited sources. RECOMMENDATION: Either cite an FCC/OET bulletin or EPA radtown page, or remove the absolute comparison and state 'frequencies are in the same range as common household wireless devices.'

Claim 18-3: Smart meters provide fewer estimated bills, faster outage detection, better usage insight [CONFIRMED] — DOE grid modernization page confirms 'consumers can better manage their own energy consumption and costs because they have easier access to their own data' and 'improved security, reduced peak loads.' EIA confirms smart meters 'wirelessly send power usage data in real time.'

Claim 18-4: Smart meters 'cannot see' which exact device was used [UNVERIFIED] — This is a judgment call about NILM (non-intrusive load monitoring) technology capability. Some advanced analytics CAN identify specific devices from signature patterns (see NILM research). The page asserts this as absolute ('They cannot see: Which exact device you used'), which is contested by the engineering literature. NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW by domain expert. RECOMMENDATION: Qualify to 'Most smart meters sold to residential customers do not identify specific appliances — however, advanced analytics can infer appliance types from usage patterns with varying accuracy.'

Claim 18-5: 'A new meter can make the bill look higher even if your habits did not change. That is often a correction, not an error.' [UNVERIFIED] — While this is a commonly stated position in the industry, the page's cited sources (DOE grid modernization, EIA) do not address meter accuracy comparisons between analog and digital. No source is cited for the claim that analog meters 'can slow down as they age' or that digital meters reveal 'true usage.' NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW for substantiation. RECOMMENDATION: Add a citation from a utility industry publication or NIST study on meter accuracy comparisons.
--- PAGE #19: 19-utility-bill-surcharges-and-riders-explained.md ---

Claim 19-1: DOE electricity-bill guidance explains that bills can be reproduced using the applicable rate structure and measured energy use/demand [CONFIRMED] — The DOE 'Evaluating Your Utility Rate Options' page at https://www.energy.gov/cmei/femp/evaluating-your-utility-rate-options retrieved 2026-08-29 discusses rate components and how 'Electric utility costs are determined by a site's load magnitude and shape and its utility bill structure.' The claimed PDF (Better Buildings Solution Center) could not be fetched due to SSL error, but the DOE rate options page broadly supports the statement about reproducible billing.

Claim 19-2: DOE note that utility rate options and bill components can be determined differently and can be affected differently by changes in use [CONFIRMED] — The same DOE rate options page states: 'A site's utility bill typically has several cost components, each of which is determined differently. Changes in electricity use from energy efficiency measures or on-site generation projects impact the charges differently.'

Claim 19-3: The page defines 'surcharge' or 'rider' from authoritative sources [REFUTED] — Neither cited source (DOE PDF, DOE Evaluating Your Utility Rate Options) contains a formal definition of 'surcharge' or 'rider.' The DOE rate options page uses terms like 'fixed charges,' 'demand charges,' and 'energy charges' but does not use 'surcharge' or 'rider' as defined terms. The page's approach — verifying surcharges/riders against the tariff — is valid utility practice, but it does not cite an authoritative source that defines what a surcharge or rider IS. The page title promises definitions but delivers procedure. RECOMMENDATION: Either add NARUC glossary definitions or acknowledge that surcharge/rider have no single regulatory definition and vary by jurisdiction. Replace 'A surcharge or rider is an account-specific bill component' with a more accurate opening like 'The terms surcharge and rider have no universal definition — they must be interpreted from the applicable tariff.'

Claim 19-4: 'Do not assume a rider is temporary, regulatory, universal, non-negotiable, or associated with a particular program from its name alone.' [UNVERIFIED] — This is prudent advice but is not re-derived from the cited sources. The DOE rate options page does not discuss assumptions about riders' nature. This claim is practical guidance from the author, not a verified factual assertion. Marking UNVERIFIED because it cannot be confirmed against cited sources, but it is reasonable practice.
--- PAGE #20: mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms-on-gas-bill.md ---

Claim 20-1: 1 CCF = 100 cubic feet of natural gas [CONFIRMED] — EIA definition: '100 cubic feet (1 Ccf) of natural gas' from FAQ at https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=45&t=7 retrieved 2026-08-29. Also confirmed in EPA WaterSense page: 'A CCF...represents one hundred cubic feet of water.'
Claim 20-2: 1 MCF = 1,000 cubic feet of natural gas [CONFIRMED] — Same EIA FAQ source: '1,000 cubic feet (Mcf) of natural gas.'

Claim 20-3: 1 therm = 100,000 BTU [CONFIRMED] — EIA explains: 'One therm = 100,000 Btu' implicitly through the conversion. The EIA FAQ states: '100 cubic feet (1 Ccf) of natural gas equals 103,700 Btu, or 1.037 therms.' Since 1.037 therms = 103,700 Btu, then 1 therm = 100,000 Btu by definition.

Claim 20-4: 1 CCF ≈ 1.037 Therms; 1 MCF ≈ 10.37 Therms [CONFIRMED] — EIA FAQ states exactly: '100 cubic feet (1 Ccf) of natural gas equals 103,700 Btu, or 1.037 therms. 1,000 cubic feet (Mcf) of natural gas equals 1.037 MMBtu, or 10.37 therms.' The page's conversion table exactly matches EIA values. Precision: EIA uses 1,037 Btu/cf (2025 annual average), which matches the page's stated 1 CCF = 103,700 BTU = 1.037 therms.

Claim 20-5: Regional preference statements — CCF common in Midwest/Northeast, therms standard in California/West [UNVERIFIED] — The page states: 'CCF is more common' in Midwest/Northeast; 'therms are the dominant unit' in Western states, particularly California with CPUC regulation. The page has NO cited sources for these regional claims. The EIA data confirms that states use different billing units, but no authoritative source is cited in the page. The frontmatter has no `sources:` key — the page provides no external references at all. NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: Check against EIA state-by-state billing unit data or CPUC regulations. The claim about CPUC 'standardizing energy billing' is plausible but unverified.

Claim 20-6: Typical $/therm and $/unit sanity ranges — The page gives example rates of $0.96-1.06/therm [UNVERIFIED against explicit cost data from this page, but cross-checkable against EIA] — EIA data (May 2026 US average residential price: $19.83/MCF) = $19.83 ÷ 10.37 therms/MCF = $1.91/therm national average. The page's example of $0.96-1.06/therm is significantly BELOW the national average of ~$1.91/therm. However, EIA data shows wide state variation: Idaho $10.82/MCF = $1.04/therm, California $22.45-23.78/MCF = $2.16-2.29/therm. The page's examples are in the range of low-cost states (Idaho, Montana, North Dakota) but are not representative of national averages. This could mislead readers into thinking $0.96/therm is a typical benchmark. RECOMMENDATION: Either add 'These are examples only — actual rates vary widely by state' with citation to EIA data, or update the example to reflect the national average of roughly $1.80-2.00/therm.
--- CROSS-CUTTING FINDINGS ---

Finding A: Page #20 has ZERO outbound source URLs in its frontmatter — the `sources:` key is absent entirely. This is a critical credibility risk for the site's AdSense re-approval mission. All conversion factor claims happen to be correct (confirmed against EIA), but no reader can verify this from the page. RECOMMENDATION: Add `sources:` to frontmatter with links to https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=45&t=7 and https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/units-and-calculators/british-thermal-units.php

Finding B: Page #19's 92.9% bounce / 8s TOP is consistent with its content. The page title promises 'Surcharges and Riders Explained' but the quick answer is a procedural guide ('verify against tariff'), not an explanation. Readers who bounce are looking for definitions — the page gives them a workflow. This is a content-audience mismatch. RECOMMENDATION: Add a bullet list of what surcharges/riders ARE (e.g., 'A rider is a temporary or permanent adjustment to the base tariff rate, approved by the PUC, to recover specific costs') before the procedure.

Finding C: The hint about 'author/editor identity claims are under review' is not triggered for these pages — all three claim authorship by Margaret Harrington or Tanya Patterson, plausible names with no obvious falsification.
